title: Islamic Manners and Etiquette
description:
Islamic manners (adab) are an integral part of faith, encompassing every aspect of a Muslim's daily life from eating and speaking to interactions with others. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said: 'I was sent to perfect good character' (Sahih al-Bukhari 60). This course explores the comprehensive system of etiquette taught in the Quran and Sunnah, demonstrating how Islamic manners elevate daily activities into acts of worship.

Drawing from authentic hadith collections and classical works on adab such as Imam al-Nawawi's Riyad al-Salihin and Imam al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din, this course covers the etiquette of eating, drinking, speaking, greeting, visiting, and daily interactions. Each lesson provides practical guidance rooted in prophetic example, showing how small behavioral changes can transform a Muslim's character and relationships.

The course emphasizes that Islamic manners are not mere social conventions but expressions of faith and gratitude to Allah. By following the prophetic example in everyday actions, Muslims demonstrate their love for the Prophet (peace be upon him) and their commitment to living as Allah commands. The result is a life of beauty, purpose, and blessing that benefits both the individual and the community.
short_description: Master the beautiful system of Islamic manners (adab) from the Quran and Sunnah for everyday life.

modules.title: The Foundations of Islamic Manners
modules.description: Understand the importance of adab in Islam, its relationship to faith, and the prophetic model of excellent character.

lessons.title: What is Adab? The Islamic Concept of Manners
lessons.content:
The Arabic word 'adab' (أدب) encompasses much more than what the English word 'manners' conveys. Linguistically, it refers to something that disciplines and beautifies character. In Islamic terminology, adab is the comprehensive system of behavior that governs a Muslim's interactions with Allah, with other people, and with the creation. It includes humility, respect, kindness, gratitude, and awareness of proper conduct in every situation.

The importance of adab in Islam is underscored by numerous Quranic verses and hadith. Allah says: 'Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often' (Quran 33:21). The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) embodied perfect adab in every aspect of his life, from his prayer to his speech to his treatment of others.

Imam al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH) devoted an entire section of his masterwork, Ihya Ulum al-Din, to the 'Etiquettes of Eating and Drinking,' explaining that even the most mundane activities can become acts of worship when performed with proper adab. He wrote: 'The one who eats with adab eats as if he is performing an act of worship, while the one who eats without adab eats as if he is merely satisfying an animal desire.'

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Nothing is heavier on the believer's Scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. Indeed, Allah hates the obscene, foul-mouthed person' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2002). This hadith establishes that good manners are not optional embellishments but essential components of faith that directly affect a person's ultimate destiny. The scholars note that adab is so important because it reflects the inner state of the heart: good manners flow from a heart that is sound and connected to Allah.

lessons.title: The Prophetic Model of Excellent Character
lessons.content:
The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the ultimate example of perfect character and manners. His wife Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) was asked about his character, and she replied: 'His character was the Quran' (Sahih Muslim 746). This means that he embodied every virtue mentioned in the Quran: patience, kindness, generosity, forgiveness, and justice.

The companions described various aspects of the Prophet's manners. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him), who served the Prophet for ten years, said: 'He never said to me, 'Why did you do this?' or 'Why didn't you do that?'' (Sahih Muslim 2309). This shows his extraordinary patience and forbearance with others. Abdullah ibn Harith reported: 'I have never seen anyone more smiling in face than the Messenger of Allah' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2018). His constant smile put people at ease and reflected his inner peace and kindness.

The Prophet's manners extended to every detail of life. He would not sit down until those around him had sat. He would not begin eating before those at his table. He would visit the sick, attend funerals, and help with manual labor. When he greeted someone, he would turn his entire body toward them, showing complete attention and respect. These small actions demonstrate that true adab is not about formal etiquette alone but about genuine care and consideration for others.

Imam al-Nawawi (d. 676 AH) compiled many of these prophetic manners in his famous work Riyad al-Salihin (Gardens of the Righteous), organizing them into categories that cover every aspect of daily life. He emphasized that following the Prophet's example in matters of adab is itself an act of worship, as it fulfills the command to follow the Messenger. By studying and emulating the prophetic model, Muslims develop character that is pleasing to Allah and beneficial to all of creation.

lessons.title: The Relationship Between Iman and Adab
lessons.content:
In Islam, faith (iman) and manners (adab) are inseparable. Good character is not merely a social nicety but a manifestation of true faith. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The most complete of the believers in faith are those with the best character' (Sunan Abu Dawud 4682). This hadith establishes a direct connection between the quality of one's faith and the quality of one's manners.

Imam al-Bukhari titled a chapter in his Sahih: 'Good Manners Are Part of Faith,' citing the hadith: 'Modesty is a branch of faith' (Sahih Muslim 35). The scholars explained that this means every virtue associated with good manners—humility, patience, kindness, generosity, honesty—is an integral part of faith, not separate from it. A person whose faith increases will naturally develop better character, and a person who improves their character will find their faith increasing.

The Quran describes the believers as those who 'spend [in the cause of Allah] in ease and hardship and those who restrain anger and pardon people. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good' (Quran 3:134). Notice how spending (an act of worship), restraining anger (a matter of character), and pardoning others (a social virtue) are all mentioned together as qualities of the believers. This integration of worship and character is a hallmark of Islamic teaching.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728 AH) explained that the relationship between iman and adab is one of cause and effect. When the heart is truly connected to Allah through faith, it naturally produces good character because the believer becomes aware of Allah's presence in every situation. This awareness (muraqaba) motivates the person to behave with the best manners, knowing that Allah is watching. Thus, improving one's character is both a sign of faith and a means of strengthening it, creating a virtuous cycle that elevates the Muslim to higher spiritual ranks.

modules.title: Adab of Eating and Drinking
modules.description: Learn the beautiful etiquette of eating and drinking as taught by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

lessons.title: Before Eating: Bismillah and Gratitude
lessons.content:
Islam elevates the simple act of eating into an act of worship through a beautiful system of etiquette that begins before the first bite. The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught: 'When any of you eats, let him mention the name of Allah. If he forgets at the beginning, let him say: Bismillahi awwalahu wa akhirahu (In the name of Allah at its beginning and its end)' (Sunan Abu Dawud 3767). This hadith shows that even forgetting is forgiven, and the name of Allah can be invoked at any point during the meal.

The scholars explain that saying 'Bismillah' (بسم الله) before eating serves multiple purposes. First, it reminds the eater that the food is a gift from Allah, fostering gratitude. Second, it seeks Allah's blessings (barakah) in the food. Third, it distinguishes the Muslim's eating from the practice of those who do not acknowledge Allah's provision. Imam al-Nawawi noted that even if one is eating alone, saying Bismillah is recommended because the angels are always present and because the practice disciplines the soul.

Before eating, the Prophet (peace be upon him) would also say: 'Allahumma barik lana fima razaqtana wa qina 'adhab-an-nar' (O Allah, bless us in what You have provided us and protect us from the Hellfire) (Sunan Ibn Majah 3324). This dua encapsulates the Muslim's relationship with food: seeking blessing in provision and protection from punishment. It transforms a routine activity into a moment of spiritual connection.

The etiquette also includes washing hands before and after eating, sitting on the floor (when possible), and eating with the right hand. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you eats, let him eat with his right hand, and when he drinks, let him drink with his right hand, for Shaytan eats and drinks with his left hand' (Sahih Muslim 2020). These seemingly small acts of adab train the Muslim in mindfulness, gratitude, and following the sunnah in every detail of life.

lessons.title: During the Meal: Sunnahs and Manners
lessons.content:
The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) provided detailed guidance on how to eat, turning every aspect of the meal into a practice of good character. Among the most important manners during the meal is eating from what is directly in front of you. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you eats, let him not touch the serving dish in the middle, for the blessing descends in the middle of the dish' (Sahih Muslim 2012). This practice teaches contentment, prevents greed, and ensures that everyone at the table is treated fairly.

Another important sunnah is to lick one's fingers clean. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'When one of you eats, let him lick his fingers, for he does not know where the blessing lies' (Sahih Muslim 2033). This hadith teaches that even the last traces of food on one's fingers may carry barakah (blessing), so one should not waste anything. It also teaches gratitude for every morsel of provision from Allah.

The Prophet also advised against blowing on hot food. When asked about this, he said: 'Do not blow on food and drink, for the blessing is in it' (Sunan Abu Dawud 3719). Instead, he would wait for it to cool naturally or fan it with his hand. The scholars interpreted this as both preserving the blessing in the food and maintaining dignity during the meal.

Eating slowly and deliberately, rather than hurriedly, is another important aspect of eating adab. The Prophet (peace be upon him) observed a man eating quickly and said: 'Why are you eating like this? On the Day of Resurrection, you will only eat as you ate in this world' (reported by al-Bayhaqi, Hasan). This hadith establishes that our eating habits in this life are connected to our status in the Hereafter, motivating Muslims to eat with mindfulness, moderation, and proper etiquette.

lessons.title: After Eating: Gratitude and Sharing
lessons.content:
The etiquette of eating does not end with the last bite. Islam teaches that after eating, a Muslim should express gratitude to Allah and share with others. The Prophet (peace be upon him) would lick his fingers, then lick the plate, and then say: 'You do not know where the blessing lies' (Sahih Muslim 2033). This practice of cleaning the plate teaches contentment, prevents waste, and shows appreciation for Allah's provision.

After eating, the sunnah is to say: 'Alhamdulillahilladhi at'amani hadha wa razaqanihi min ghayri hawlin minni wa la quwwah' (Praise be to Allah who fed me this and provided it for me without any power or strength from me) (Sunan Abu Dawud 3850). This supplication acknowledges that the ability to eat and the food itself are both gifts from Allah, reinforcing the Muslim's dependence on and gratitude to their Creator.

The scholars also emphasize the importance of sharing food with others. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'He is not a believer whose stomach is filled while his neighbor goes hungry' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6019). This hadith connects eating etiquette to social responsibility, showing that Islamic manners extend beyond personal behavior to communal welfare. Sharing food is not just a social nicety but a requirement of faith.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 751 AH) summarized the sunnahs of eating beautifully: the Muslim eats with the right hand, says Bismillah, eats from what is in front of them, licks the fingers, praises Allah after eating, and shares with others. He noted that these small practices, when consistently followed, train the soul in gratitude, humility, and generosity—virtues that extend far beyond the dining table into every aspect of life. The beauty of Islamic adab is that it transforms even the most basic human activity into a comprehensive training in character.

modules.title: Adab of Speech and Communication
modules.description: Master the Islamic guidelines for speaking truthfully, kindly, and effectively in all interactions.

lessons.title: Speaking the Truth with Wisdom
lessons.content:
Truthful speech is the foundation of Islamic manners, but Islam teaches that truth must be accompanied by wisdom and kindness. Allah commands in the Quran: 'O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true' (Quran 9:119). The word 'true' (sadiqin) implies not only speaking the truth but living it consistently. However, truth does not give permission to be harsh or insensitive.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6018). This comprehensive hadith establishes two options for the believer: speak something beneficial and good, or remain silent. There is no third option of speaking harmfully or foolishly. Imam al-Nawawi explained that 'good speech' includes truth, kindness, benefit, and what is pleasing to Allah, while silence is preferred when speech lacks these qualities.

The scholars have identified conditions for proper speech: it should be true, beneficial, necessary (or at least not harmful), and spoken with the right intention and in the right manner. Sometimes the truth can be spoken in a way that causes unnecessary harm, while a gentle approach can achieve the same goal. Allah says: 'And speak to people with good words' (Quran 2:83), indicating that the manner of speaking is as important as the content.

Imam al-Ghazali devoted an entire chapter of his Ihya to the 'Etiquettes of the Tongue,' warning against lying, backbiting, gossip, slander,Mockery, and argumentation. He explained that the tongue is the interpreter of the heart, and its corruption reflects spiritual disease. By disciplining the tongue through truthfulness and wisdom, the believer purifies the heart and draws closer to Allah.

lessons.title: Avoiding Harmful Speech: Gossip, Backbiting, and Slander
lessons.content:
Islam places tremendous emphasis on avoiding harmful speech, considering it a serious sin that destroys social bonds and spiritual health. The most commonly warned-against forms of harmful speech are gossip (ghiba), backbiting (nameema), and slander (buhtan). Allah describes backbiting vividly in the Quran: 'Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead? You would detest it' (Quran 49:12). This powerful metaphor illustrates the ugliness of speaking behind someone's back.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) defined backbiting when asked by his companions: 'Do you know what backbiting is?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'Mentioning your brother in a way he would dislike.' They asked: 'What if what I say about my brother is true?' He said: 'If what you say is true, then you have backbitten him, and if it is not true, then you have slandered him' (Sahih Muslim 2589). This definition shows that even truthful negative speech about an absent person constitutes backbiting.

The scholars distinguished between backbiting (mentioning someone's faults to a third party) and slander (fabricating lies about someone). Both are major sins, but slander is considered worse because it combines lying with harming reputation. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The curse of Allah is upon the one who insults his Muslim brother' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 1961).

Exceptions to the prohibition of mentioning someone's faults include: seeking help against oppression, warning others about dangerous individuals, and seeking a legal ruling from a scholar. However, these exceptions are narrowly defined and must be handled with care. Imam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 852 AH) emphasized that even in these cases, one should mention only what is necessary and avoid embellishment. The general rule remains: protect the honor of others as you would protect your own, for 'the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand the Muslims are safe' (Sahih al-Bukhari 10).

These guidelines for speech create a community built on trust, respect, and genuine care for one another's reputation and well-being.

lessons.title: The Power of Gentle and Kind Speech
lessons.content:
Islam teaches that gentle, kind speech is not only a manner but a powerful tool for guidance and relationship building. Allah describes the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as being sent with 'a clear warner and a caller to Allah by His permission and a illuminating lamp' (Quran 33:46), and His manner of calling was characterized by gentleness. Allah commands: 'And speak to people with good words' (Quran 2:83).

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Nothing is heavier on the believer's Scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. Indeed, Allah hates the obscene, foul-mouthed person' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2002). He also said: 'The most beloved of you to me and the closest of you to me in座位 on the Day of Resurrection are those with the best character' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2018). These hadith establish that kind speech is a primary marker of faith and a means of earning Allah's love.

The power of gentle speech is illustrated in the story of Prophet Musa (Moses) when he was commanded to speak to Pharaoh. Allah told him: 'And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear Allah' (Quran 20:44). If a tyrant like Pharaoh deserved gentle speech, how much more so do ordinary people in our daily interactions? The scholars note that gentleness does not mean weakness or compromising truth, but delivering truth in the most effective and dignified manner.

Imam al-Hasan al-Basri (d. 110 AH) was known for his gentle speech even when correcting others. He said: 'Make your speech gentle, and you will win hearts. Make it harsh, and you will drive people away.' Modern communication research confirms this wisdom: people are more receptive to messages delivered with kindness and respect. The Islamic approach to speech combines spiritual reward with practical effectiveness, creating a communication style that is both pleasing to Allah and beneficial to human relationships.

modules.title: Adab of Daily Interactions
modules.description: Learn the etiquettes of greeting, visiting, entering and leaving homes, and other daily interactions.

lessons.title: The Greeting of Peace (Salam)
lessons.content:
The greeting of Islam, 'As-salamu alaykum' (السلام عليكم - Peace be upon you), is one of the most distinctive features of Muslim identity and one of the most emphasized manners in the Quran and Sunnah. Allah commands: 'And when you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it or return it equally. Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, an Accountant' (Quran 4:86). This verse establishes that responding to the greeting of peace is an obligation, and responding with something better is rewarded.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not tell you of something that, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the Salam among yourselves' (Sahih Muslim 54). This hadith connects the greeting of peace directly to faith and mutual love, showing that it is not merely a social convention but a spiritual practice that strengthens the bonds of the Muslim community.

The scholars have detailed the proper etiquette of giving and receiving Salam. When entering a gathering, one should say 'As-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh' (Peace, mercy, and blessings of Allah be upon you). The response should be at least as good as the greeting, and preferably better. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The best of people are those who are most generous in giving Salam' (Sunan Abu Dawud 4800). Starting the greeting first is preferred over waiting to be greeted, as it demonstrates initiative in spreading peace.

Imam al-Nawawi noted that the Salam is unique to Islam and serves as a marker of Muslim identity. When Muslims greet each other with 'As-salamu alaykum,' they are not merely saying hello but invoking Allah's peace upon one another. This practice creates an atmosphere of trust, safety, and brotherhood wherever Muslims gather. In our modern world of digital communication, the prophetic emphasis on spreading Salam reminds us of the importance of personal, warm, and meaningful interactions in building a cohesive community.

lessons.title: Adab of Visiting and Hosting
lessons.content:
Visiting one another (ziyara) and hosting guests (diyafa) are important acts of worship in Islam that strengthen community bonds and earn great rewards. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him be generous to his neighbor. Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him be generous to his guest' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6136). Generosity to guests is placed on the same level as faith itself.

When visiting someone, the Prophet (peace be upon him) taught that one should ask permission before entering. Allah says: 'O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess and those who have not [yet] reached puberty among you ask permission of you [before entering] at three times: before the dawn prayer and when [you put aside] your garments [for rest] at noon and after the night prayer. These are three times of privacy for you. There is no blame upon you nor upon them beyond these [periods], for they continually circulate among you and you among them' (Quran 24:58). The general principle of asking permission extends to all visits.

The host's etiquette includes preparing for the guest's comfort, offering food and drink, and making them feel welcome. The Prophet (peace be upon him) would give the best seat to his guest and give them preference over himself. When the Prophet was offered the choice between a bowl of milk and a bowl of meat, he would choose the milk, then invite others to share. The guest's etiquette includes eating what is offered, making dua for the host, and not overstaying one's welcome.

The reward for proper hosting is immense. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. The right of a guest is that he should be honored for one day and night, and hospitality is for three days. Anything beyond that is charity' (Sahih Muslim 1427). Three days is the maximum period of honor, after which the guest should consider their departure to avoid burdening the host. These guidelines create a system of hospitality that is generous yet sustainable, strengthening the bonds of Muslim brotherhood and sisterhood.

lessons.title: Entering and Leaving the Home
lessons.content:
Islam provides specific guidance for entering and leaving one's home, transforming these routine actions into acts of worship and protection. The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught: 'When a man enters his home, let him say: Bismillah wadakhaltu, Bismillah kharajtu, wa 'ala Allahi rabbina tawakkaltu (In the name of Allah I enter, in the name of Allah I leave, and upon Allah, my Lord, I rely). When he enters, let him not disturb his family. When he leaves, let him say the same' (Sunan Abu Dawud 5095). This dua establishes the home as a place of divine protection and reliance on Allah.

When leaving the home, the Prophet (peace be upon him) would also say: 'Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'ala Allah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah' (In the name of Allah, I place my trust in Allah, and there is no power nor might except with Allah) (Sunan Abu Dawud 5095). When returning, he would say: 'A'taytukum, Allahumma ajirni minash-shaytan' (I have returned, O Allah, I seek refuge in You from Shaytan) (Sunan Abu Dawud 5096). These remembrances bookend one's time outside the home with prayers for protection and reliance on Allah.

The scholars explain that these adab serve multiple purposes. Spiritually, they remind the Muslim that their home is under Allah's protection and that they should enter with good intentions and leave with good prayers. Practically, they create a habit of dhikr (remembrance) that integrates faith into daily routines. Psychologically, they provide a sense of security and purpose in one's comings and goings.

Imam al-Bukhari included in his Sahih that when one knocks on a door, they should not look inside until given permission, and when one enters, they should say 'As-salamu alaykum.' These additional etiquettes extend the respect for privacy and the greeting of peace to every home one visits. The comprehensive nature of these guidelines shows that Islam considers the home sacred space worthy of special reverence, and that one's behavior in entering and leaving reflects their respect for both the home and its inhabitants.
